description:
We are a team of curious minds, problem-solvers, and technology enthusiasts passionate about exploring the intersection of science, space, and innovation.

We value collaboration over competition, curiosity over assumptions, and experimentation over perfection. Our goal is not just to participate but to build something impactful, learn from diverse perspectives, and push the boundaries of what we can achieve together.
summary:
We are developing SPHEREx Explorer, a public-facing web application that transforms NASA's SPHEREx astronomical observations into an accessible platform for discovering moving and variable celestial objects. Users can enter Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec) coordinates to retrieve observations of specific sky regions across different dates and visualize them through interactive time-lapse animations.

The platform integrates SPHEREx data releases, processes FITS images, organizes observations across six detector arrays, and applies scientifically compatible image co-adding techniques to improve the signal-to-noise ratio of faint astronomical sources. Additional capabilities include image blinking, subtraction, multi-band infrared visualization, and AI-assisted identification of potential moving objects and brightness variations.

By simplifying access to complex astronomical datasets, SPHEREx Explorer bridges the gap between professional astronomy and citizen science. It empowers researchers, students, and astronomy enthusiasts to explore massive volumes of space data, identify interesting celestial phenomena, and contribute to future astronomical discoveries.
details:
1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

SPHEREx Explorer is a web-based astronomical discovery platform designed to make NASA's SPHEREx observations easier to explore and analyze. SPHEREx scans the entire sky in 102 near-infrared spectral bands, creating a valuable dataset for studying celestial objects and their changes over time.

Our platform allows users to enter Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec) coordinates to search for a specific region of the sky. It retrieves available SPHEREx observations from different dates, organizes the images by observation time, detector, and wavelength, and presents them through an interactive visualization interface.

Users can explore observations using time-lapse animations, image blinking, image subtraction, and multi-band comparisons. The platform also aims to support image co-addition to improve the signal-to-noise ratio of compatible observations and AI-assisted identification of potential moving or variable objects.

2. What benefits does it offer?

  • Simplified data access: Makes complex astronomical observations accessible through a user-friendly interface.
  • Time-domain exploration: Helps users identify changes in celestial objects by comparing observations from different dates.
  • Improved image quality: Scientifically compatible observations can be combined to improve the visibility of faint sources.
  • Multi-wavelength analysis: Enables exploration of infrared observations across different spectral bands.
  • Research and education: Provides students, researchers, and astronomy enthusiasts with an interactive way to investigate real space data.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to bridge the gap between large-scale astronomical datasets and public participation in scientific discovery. By transforming SPHEREx observations into an interactive exploration experience, the project can help researchers and citizen scientists investigate transient events, variable stars, moving objects, and other interesting astronomical phenomena.

In the long term, the platform could support collaborative discovery, encourage data-driven astronomy education, and make future SPHEREx data releases easier to explore.

4. What tools, programming languages, and software are used?

The project is designed around an open-source technology stack:

  • Programming language: Python for data retrieval, scientific processing, and backend development; JavaScript/TypeScript for the web interface.
  • Backend: FastAPI for building APIs and managing observation requests.
  • Astronomy libraries: Astropy and PyVO for coordinate validation, astronomical data access, and FITS processing.
  • Image processing: NumPy, SciPy, OpenCV, and Reproject for image analysis, alignment, and compatible image co-addition.
  • Visualization: React, Plotly, and Aladin Lite for interactive sky exploration and time-based visualization.
  • Data source: NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) SPHEREx observations.
  • AI/ML: Scikit-learn and PyTorch for future automated source detection and anomaly identification.
  • Data storage: PostgreSQL for observation metadata and file/object storage for astronomical image products.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

The creative aspect lies in turning a massive scientific dataset into an interactive astronomical time machine. Instead of simply displaying static images, SPHEREx Explorer allows users to investigate how a selected region of the sky changes across multiple observations.

The combination of coordinate-based searching, time-lapse visualization, multi-wavelength exploration, image comparison, and AI-assisted analysis creates a unified discovery workflow. Another important feature is the ability to preserve observations from different epochs while combining only scientifically compatible images for improved signal quality.

6. What factors did the team consider?

Our team considered several scientific and technical factors:

  • Scientific accuracy: Different detector arrays and wavelength bands must not be combined indiscriminately. Only compatible observations should be co-added.
  • Time-based consistency: Original observation dates must be preserved to avoid losing information about moving or variable objects.
  • Data quality: Calibration information, exposure differences, contamination flags, and quality masks must be considered during image processing.
  • Scalability: The architecture should accommodate future SPHEREx data releases without requiring major changes.
  • Accessibility: The platform should be usable by people without advanced astronomy or programming knowledge.
  • Performance: Data retrieval, image processing, and visualization should remain efficient as the dataset grows.

Ultimately, SPHEREx Explorer aims to make astronomical exploration more interactive, accessible, and collaborative by connecting NASA's infrared observations with modern web technologies and AI-assisted scientific analysis.
